sentences.text: Signe was eleven and lived in Bergen, on the wet green west coast of Norway.
Her father was a schoolteacher and her mother worked at an insurance office and neither of them was, in any sense, a country person.

But her father's older brother, her uncle Ólafur, was — Ólafur was a sheep farmer, and had been all his life, on a narrow green shelf of land above the Nærøyfjord, one of the deepest and narrowest fjords on the whole west coast.
It was three hours by car and boat from Bergen.
Ólafur had never married.
He lived alone in a small red-painted wooden farmhouse with a barn and a wood-fired kitchen and three hundred sheep.
He had inherited the farm from his own father, who had inherited it from his father, who had cleared the shelf of trees a hundred and forty years ago.
Every July, Signe went for three weeks.
She had first gone when she was six, with her father, and had loved it enough to keep going every year since.
This July she was eleven, and she was — for the first time — considered old enough to help with the sheep on the high pastures.
That was the plan for the summer.
Ólafur was in his early fifties.
He had a short greying blond beard, and pale grey eyes, and hands that had lifted lambs out of ewes for thirty years and looked like it.
He was quieter even than Signe's father, which was saying something.
He did not chat, ever.
He said what needed to be said.
When Signe asked him a question, he thought about the answer for as long as it took, and then he gave it in as few words as possible.
Signe had learned, over five summers, that this was not because Ólafur did not care.
It was because Ólafur believed that words used up something in the world, and that they should be spent carefully.
In the traditional Norwegian way, Ólafur's sheep spent the summer up on the fjellbeite — the high mountain pastures above the fjord.
In late June each year he drove them up the steep trail behind the farm, past the tree line, and released them onto the alpine grass.
There they roamed freely for two and a half months, feeding on the fresh summer grass and the small alpine herbs that made Norwegian mutton famous.
Ólafur went up every four or five days to check them, walking the long high loops of the ridge.
In late August or early September he brought them down again.
That was the year's rhythm.
Signe helped with the daily work on the farm — feeding the chickens, mending the low stone walls, oiling Ólafur's tools, making bread with him in the wood-fired oven.
In her second week, Ólafur said, at breakfast, "On Friday I am going up to check the high pasture.
You will come with me.
It is a long walk.
Wear the good boots.
Bring your rain trousers." Signe was very pleased.
She had asked to go up every year and every year Ólafur had said, next year.
Thursday afternoon, they made preparations.

Ólafur packed a small hard bag with a flask of coffee, some hard bread and brown cheese, a small first-aid kit, a length of thin rope, a compass, a folded map of the ridge, and a small radio for weather updates.
He took his own staff — a long curved shepherd's staff made of dark birchwood, with a black iron hook at the end.
It was as tall as he was.
It looked ancient.
Signe asked about it.
Ólafur said, "My grandfather made it.
Nineteen twenty-eight.
He was your age when he cut the wood.
The iron hook was already old — from a farm implement his own grandfather had.
So the staff is a hundred years old and the hook is older.
Passed to my father, then to me.
It works." He turned it around in his hands.
On the shaft, near the top, Signe could see, burned into the wood, two small letters — OT.
"Olav Torgersen," Ólafur said.
"His mark.
On everything he made."
That evening Ólafur turned on the small radio and listened to the coastal weather forecast, as he did every evening.
He listened for a long time.
When it was over, he said to Signe, "There is a summer storm moving in tomorrow afternoon.
Not too bad — thunder, hard rain, maybe two hours.
Nothing dangerous down here.
But on the ridge, weather is always more.
We go early tomorrow.
We check the sheep quickly.
If they are where they should be, we come straight back down.
If any are missing, we deal with that.
Then home before the rain."
Signe said, "Are the sheep in danger from thunder?" Ólafur said, "Not usually.
They know to find shelter.
They have been on that ridge for a thousand years.
What I worry about, when there is thunder, is Ester." He drank his coffee.
Signe waited.
He said, "Ester is old.
Eight years.
Old for a mountain ewe.
She is the smartest sheep I have.
She always leads the others down when the weather is bad.
That is her role in the flock.
If the flock is under a rock overhang tomorrow, she is the reason.
But she is also curious.
She wanders.
Sometimes I find her in strange places.
If she is not with the others tomorrow, I want to know why."
They left at six in the morning.
The trail up from the farm was a hard steep zig-zag cut into the side of the mountain — the same trail Ólafur's grandfather and great-grandfather had used.
It took Ólafur about ninety minutes to climb at his own pace.
It took Signe closer to two hours, at eleven.
Ólafur waited at each of the switchbacks without commenting.
He never rushed her.
She was pleased with herself for keeping up as well as she did.
At the top of the climb, the trail opened out onto the high pasture — a wide gently sloping green shelf that ran along the top of the fjord for several kilometers before rising into higher rock.
It was cool, and the wind was fresh, and the sky was pale grey with a heavier line of cloud on the western horizon.
Ólafur stopped and scanned the pasture with his small binoculars.
Signe stood beside him and looked too.
There were sheep scattered across the green — perhaps a hundred and fifty of them visible from where they stood.
Others were probably around the bend or in the low folds.
But even from here Signe could see they were unsettled — bunched, not grazing, heads up.
They already knew the weather was changing.
